summary: Emil Kowalski explains how he built Vaul, an open-source drawer (bottom sheet) for the web modelled on Apple's iOS Sheet. He covers the anatomy (built on Radix's Dialog primitive with a Radix-like API), a drag gesture that must not drop frames, momentum and damping, how scrolling and dragging coexist, scaling the page behind the drawer, the iOS-matched curve and 500ms duration, handling the virtual keyboard with the Visual Viewport API, ignoring extra touches, snap points, syncing Safari's theme bar, and testing on real devices. For a design system it is a concrete checklist of the invisible details that make a sheet feel native, with exact motion values, performance traps and interaction thresholds.
key_ideas: On mobile a drawer feels more native than a modal.
Build on an accessible dialog primitive (Radix Dialog) and mirror its API so the component feels familiar.
Changing an inherited CSS variable on every drag frame forces style recalculation for all children; set transform directly on the element instead.
Momentum-based dragging lets a flick close the drawer; damping past the top makes it feel physical because real things slow down before stopping.
Only allow dragging when scrolled to the top, and block drag for 100ms after reaching the top so a fast scroll cannot close the drawer.
The drawer uses cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) from the Ionic Framework and 500ms to mimic the iOS Sheet; easing and duration make a big difference to how any component feels.
Background scale and corner radius follow drag progress while dragging.
Handle the virtual keyboard with the Visual Viewport API so the drawer sits above the keyboard and stays fully scrollable.
Ignore extra touches after the first to stop the drawer jumping.
Snap points snap to the closest point on release, can be viewport fractions or fixed pixels, and respect momentum.
Safari's theme bar cannot transition or use transparency, so compute the opaque overlay colour and step it with the same curve as the drawer.
Invisible details matter because they match users' expectations from native OS drawers.
Debug on a real phone (or Xcode Simulator), not a shrunken desktop window.

rules.rule: On mobile, present content in a drawer (bottom sheet) rather than a modal.
rules.why: A drawer gives a more native feel on mobile.
rules.evidence: Why a drawer?

rules.rule: Give drawers drag-to-dismiss.
rules.why: The previous Vercel drawer lacked drag-to-dismiss, one of the reasons Vaul was built.
rules.evidence: lacked drag-to-dismiss functionality

rules.rule: Build the drawer on an accessible dialog primitive such as Radix's Dialog.
rules.why: Radix ensures the component is accessible and handles focus management.
rules.evidence: Anatomy

rules.rule: Mirror the underlying primitive's API with compound parts: Drawer.Root wrapping Drawer.Trigger and Drawer.Portal, with Drawer.Content and Drawer.Overlay rendered inside Drawer.Portal.
rules.why: An API very similar to Radix's feels familiar.
rules.evidence: Anatomy

rules.rule: Keep the drag gesture at full frame rate; do not drop frames while dragging.
rules.why: The author calls not losing frames while dragging 'a good start' and describes his own dropped frames as a failure.
rules.evidence: Not losing frames while dragging is a good start, but I already failed there.

rules.rule: Update the drag position without triggering component re-renders.
rules.why: The author's drag already avoided re-renders, which he treats as the expected cause of dropped frames ('so what could cause it to drop frames?').
rules.evidence: Dragging was done without any re-renders, so what could cause it to drop frames?

rules.rule: Do not drive the drag position through an inherited CSS custom property (such as --swipe-amount) set on the drawer.
rules.why: CSS variables are inheritable, so each change triggers style recalculation for all children; the drag became laggy once content passed about 20 list items.
rules.evidence: Since CSS Variables are inheritable

rules.rule: Set the drag offset directly on the moving element as an inline transform: translateY(<draggedDistance>px).
rules.why: Updating the style directly on the element fixed the dropped frames.
rules.evidence: Updating the style directly on the element fixed the issue

rules.rule: Use momentum-based dragging so a flick can close the drawer without dragging it past a set point.
rules.why: You don't need to drag until a certain point to close the drawer; you can just flick it.
rules.evidence: I added momentum based dragging next

rules.rule: When the user drags upward while the drawer is already at its top, damp the drag: the further they drag, the less the drawer moves.
rules.why: It feels more natural, as things in real life don't suddenly stop, they slow down first.
rules.evidence: the drawer will damp the drag

rules.rule: Allow dragging the drawer only when its scrollable content is scrolled to the top (a shouldDrag check).
rules.why: Being scrollable and draggable at once is tricky, and this is very similar to how native drawers work on iOS.
rules.evidence: I’ve written a shouldDrag function that doesn’t allow you to drag unless you are scrolled to the top of the drawer.

rules.rule: After scrolling reaches the top of the drawer, block dragging for 100ms.
rules.why: Fast mobile scrolling can overshoot the top into a drag with enough velocity to accidentally close the drawer.
rules.evidence: I added a timeout of 100ms

rules.rule: Offer an opt-in option (scaleBackground) that makes the page behind the drawer look like another sheet by applying transform and border radius to a wrapper element ([vaul-drawer-wrapper]).
rules.why: It creates the illusion of the body becoming another sheet.
rules.evidence: Background animation

rules.rule: While dragging, derive the background's transform and border radius from drag progress rather than fixed values.
rules.why: The same background logic applies during drag, with values based on progress; dragging the drawer down 40% sets the radius to 60% of its max.
rules.evidence: Dragging the drawer down by 40% will change the border radius to 60%

rules.rule: Use the iOS-matching curve cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) (from the Ionic Framework) for drawer and sheet motion.
rules.why: The curve closely matches the one used in iOS, and the author says using the right easing and duration makes a big difference to how a component feels.
rules.evidence: The curve used in Vaul closely matches the one used in iOS

rules.rule: Use a 500ms duration for the drawer's transform transition.
rules.why: 500ms is meant to mimic iOS's Sheet.
rules.evidence: Duration of 500ms is also supposed to mimic iOS’s Sheet

rules.rule: Choose easing and duration deliberately for every component, not only drawers.
rules.why: Using the right easing and duration makes a big difference to how this, and any other component, feels.
rules.evidence: Motion

rules.rule: When an input inside a drawer gets focus, disable the browser's default scroll-into-view behaviour and position the drawer with the Visual Viewport API instead.
rules.why: When the virtual keyboard shows, the browser scrolls upward, pushing the drawer up and potentially hiding important content.
rules.evidence: Inputs

rules.rule: Listen for visualViewport resize; set the drawer's height to the visual viewport height minus an offset, and its bottom to the larger of (window.innerHeight minus visual viewport height) and 0, in px.
rules.why: The visual viewport height shrinks when the keyboard shows and grows when it hides, so it tells you how to update the drawer's height and position.
rules.evidence: We then use this information to update the drawer’s height and position accordingly

rules.rule: Register the visualViewport resize listener in an effect and remove it in the effect's cleanup.
rules.why: The source's React example adds the listener with window.visualViewport?.addEventListener and removes it in the returned cleanup.
rules.evidence: window.visualViewport?. removeEventListener

rules.rule: Keep the Visual Viewport approach even though the drawer's height updates with a slight delay after the keyboard appears.
rules.why: The new visual viewport height arrives only after the keyboard is fully visible; the author calls it not ideal but found this approach works best.
rules.evidence: It’s not ideal, but I found that this approach works best.

rules.rule: Place the drawer directly above the virtual keyboard while it is open.
rules.why: It keeps the drawer fully scrollable, which would not be the case with the browser's default behaviour.
rules.evidence: changing the position of the drawer to sit right above the keyboard

rules.rule: Ignore every touch after the first one until the user releases (for example, return early from the press handler while isDragging is true).
rules.why: Otherwise adding a second finger makes the drawer jump to the new position; the author says that if this were not addressed the drawer would feel off.
rules.evidence: Multi touch

rules.rule: Match the behaviours users expect from native OS drawers, including the small 'invisible' details.
rules.why: People use native drawers often, which creates expectations; when a feature works as assumed, users proceed without a second thought, and missing details make the drawer feel off.
rules.evidence: It’s minor, but makes a difference

rules.rule: When a drawer has snap points, on each release snap it to the point closest to its current position.
rules.why: Multiple checkpoints are a common iOS pattern, as in Apple Maps; the check runs every time you drag and release, provided snap points are specified.
rules.evidence: Snap points

rules.rule: Let snap points be set either as a fraction of the viewport or as a fixed pixel value.
rules.why: The source's snap points accept both forms.
rules.evidence: either be a fraction of the viewport or a fixed value in pixels

rules.rule: Use a fixed-pixel snap point when something such as an input must stick out by the same amount on every device.
rules.why: Fixed values ensure the content sticks out evenly on all devices.
rules.evidence: Fixed values are particularly useful

rules.rule: Make snap points momentum-based: a hard enough flick skips points or closes the drawer completely, and the same applies when dragging upward.
rules.why: The source says snap points are also momentum based, like its flick-to-close dragging.
rules.evidence: This is also momentum based

rules.rule: Match Safari's theme bar colour to the app's current background colour, including the dimmed colour while the drawer overlay is shown.
rules.why: The author wanted Safari's theme colour to match the current background colour of the app.
rules.evidence: I wanted to match Safari’s theme color with the current background color of our app.

rules.rule: To match Safari's theme bar to a semi-transparent overlay, compute the overlay's opaque equivalent on the background per channel: round(a * channel + (1 - a) * background).
rules.why: Safari's theme bar cannot use CSS transitions or semi-transparent colours.
rules.evidence: Safari Theme Bar

rules.rule: To transition the theme bar, precompute 50 interpolated colours (step factor 1 / (steps - 1), so the first and last steps are the two end colours) and update the theme-color meta tag every 10ms after the drawer opens, so the steps fill the 500ms drawer transition.
rules.why: The theme bar cannot use CSS transitions; 50 colours at 10ms each (10x50) matches the 500ms duration.
rules.evidence: I created 50 steps

rules.rule: When stepping colours for the open/close transition, interpolate along the drawer's own bezier curve (for example with the bezier-easing library), not linearly.
rules.why: Linear interpolation won't match a drawer animated with a custom bezier curve.
rules.evidence: interpolation is done using the same curve as the drawer with the help of bezier-easing

rules.rule: When interpolating theme colours, round each channel and clamp it to the 0-255 range.
rules.why: The source's interpolateColor rounds every component and clamps it below 0 and above 255.
rules.evidence: if (result[i] > 255 ) result[i] = 255 ;

rules.rule: During a drag, pick the theme colour from a linearly interpolated array by drag progress: index = floor(dragProgress * array length).
rules.why: The drag interaction needs a linear mapping from drag progress (0 to 1) to colour.
rules.evidence: We also needed a linear interpolation for the drag interaction

rules.rule: Do not ship a JavaScript-timed theme-colour transition if it falls out of step with the CSS overlay transition when frames drop.
rules.why: That mismatch is why the author has not added the theme-bar sync to Vaul.
rules.evidence: This isn’t available in Vaul yet

rules.rule: Test drawers in a real mobile environment, not by shrinking the desktop devtools window.
rules.why: A component like this needs the same environment as an actual mobile device.
rules.evidence: just simply open the dev tools and make the window smaller

rules.rule: Debug on a physical phone connected by cable, using Safari's devtools on the computer, and open the local dev server via the computer's IP address and port with both devices on the same network.
rules.why: It lets you use desktop devtools while testing on a physical phone.
rules.evidence: Most of the time, I used my phone

rules.rule: Use Xcode Simulator on macOS as an alternative test device.
rules.why: It offers a replica that matches an actual phone almost exactly.
rules.evidence: An alternative would be Xcode Simulator

rules.rule: Keep the drawer fully styleable and composable so drawers do not all have to look the same.
rules.why: Not every drawer has to look the same; Family's drawer was recreated with Vaul to show what's possible.
rules.evidence: Getting creative

rules.rule: Consider open-sourcing reusable components.
rules.why: More people use them, which brings more feedback and ultimately a better component.
rules.evidence: Open-sourcing meant that more people will use it

decisions.question: On mobile, should secondary content open in a drawer or a modal?

options.name: Drawer (bottom sheet)
options.effect: Slides up from the bottom and can be dragged or flicked away; feels native, like the iOS Sheet.
options.when: Mobile layouts where a native feel matters.

options.name: Modal
options.effect: A less native feel on mobile than a drawer, per the author's preference; the source gives no further detail about modals.
options.when: Not recommended on mobile by the source.

decisions.recommendation: Use a drawer on mobile for a more native feel.

decisions.question: Should the drawer's API be built from compound parts or configured through props?

options.name: Compound parts mirroring Radix Dialog
options.effect: Drawer.Root, Trigger, Portal, Content and Overlay; feels familiar to people who know Radix.

options.name: A single component configured with props
options.effect: Not discussed in the source [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Compound parts with an API very similar to Radix's, so it feels familiar.

decisions.question: How should the drag position be written to the page on each frame?

options.name: Inherited CSS variable (--swipe-amount) used by translateY()
options.effect: Every change recalculates styles for all children; became laggy beyond about 20 list items.

options.name: Inline transform on the moving element
options.effect: No inherited recalculation; fixed the dropped frames.
options.when: For per-frame drag updates, as in the source's drawer.

decisions.recommendation: Set transform: translateY(...) directly on the element.

decisions.question: How does a user dismiss the drawer by dragging?

options.name: Drag past a set point
options.effect: The user must drag until a certain point to close it.
options.when: The source does not recommend this alone.

options.name: Momentum-based
options.effect: A flick closes the drawer even if it has not travelled far; with snap points a hard flick can skip points.

decisions.recommendation: Momentum-based dragging, so a flick is enough.
decisions.evidence: I added momentum based dragging next

decisions.question: How should a scrollable drawer decide between scrolling its content and being dragged?

options.name: Drag only at the top, with a 100ms block after reaching it
options.effect: Works like native iOS drawers; a fast scroll that overshoots the top cannot turn into a drag that closes the drawer.

options.name: Drag only at the top, no block
options.effect: Fast mobile scrolling can carry past the top into a drag with enough velocity to accidentally close the drawer.

decisions.recommendation: Use a shouldDrag check that allows dragging only when scrolled to the top, plus a 100ms timeout after reaching the top.

decisions.question: How should the drawer respond when an input inside it opens the on-screen keyboard?

options.name: Browser default
options.effect: The browser scrolls upward, pushing the drawer up and potentially hiding content; the drawer is not fully scrollable.

options.name: Visual Viewport API
options.effect: The drawer resizes and sits right above the keyboard and stays fully scrollable, with a slight delay because the new height arrives after the keyboard is fully visible.

decisions.recommendation: Disable the browser behaviour and use the Visual Viewport API; the author found it works best despite the delay.

decisions.question: Should the page behind the drawer shrink into a sheet of its own?

options.name: Scale the background (scaleBackground)
options.effect: The body looks like another sheet: transform and border radius are applied to the wrapper, following drag progress while dragging.
options.when: When you want the layered, iOS-like sheet illusion.

options.name: Leave the background as is
options.effect: No transform or radius is applied to the page behind the drawer [inferred].
options.when: The prop is opt-in, so this is the default [inferred].

decisions.question: Should snap points be set as a fraction of the viewport or as fixed pixels?

options.name: Fraction of the viewport
options.effect: The checkpoint scales with the screen height.

options.name: Fixed pixels
options.effect: Content such as an input sticks out by the same amount on every device.
options.when: When a specific piece of content must peek out evenly on all devices.

decisions.recommendation: Fixed pixels when an input must stick out evenly on all devices; otherwise either works [inferred].

decisions.question: Should the browser's theme bar colour follow the drawer overlay?

options.name: Leave the theme bar static
options.effect: The theme bar does not change when the drawer opens; this is what Vaul shipped when the article was written.
options.when: Default, until the sync can stay in step with the overlay.

options.name: Sync via stepped theme-color updates
options.effect: 50 precomputed opaque colours, eased with the drawer's curve and updated every 10ms, linearly by progress during drag; can drift from the overlay when frames drop.
options.when: Experimental; only if it matches the overlay transition.

decisions.recommendation: The author shares the idea but has not shipped it because it does not match the overlay when frames drop.

decisions.question: Where should a drawer be tested?

options.name: Shrunk desktop devtools window
options.effect: Not the same environment as a real mobile device.
options.when: Not enough for a component like this.

options.name: Physical phone via cable with Safari devtools
options.effect: Real device behaviour with desktop devtools; load the dev server by IP and port on the same network.

options.name: Xcode Simulator
options.effect: A replica that matches an actual phone almost exactly.

decisions.recommendation: Mostly a physical phone connected to the computer, with Xcode Simulator as an alternative.

process.detail: Build the drawer on Radix's Dialog primitive for accessibility and focus management, and mirror its compound API (Root, Trigger, Portal, Content, Overlay).
Drag without re-renders and write the offset as an inline transform: translateY() on the element, not through an inherited CSS variable.
Add momentum-based dismissal so a flick closes the drawer, and damp upward drag past the top.
Allow drag only when scrolled to the top (shouldDrag) and block drag for 100ms after reaching the top.
Optionally apply transform and border radius to the wrapper element, driven by drag progress while dragging.
Transition transform over 0.5s with cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) to mimic the iOS Sheet.
Disable the browser's scroll-to-input behaviour; on visualViewport resize, set the drawer's height and bottom so it sits above the keyboard.
Ignore touches after the first until release so the drawer never jumps.
On release snap to the closest point (viewport fraction or fixed px), letting strong flicks skip points or close.

Compute the opaque overlay colour, precompute 50 eased steps, update the theme-color meta tag every 10ms on open, and pick linearly by drag progress while dragging; ship only if it stays in step with the overlay.
Connect a phone by cable, use Safari devtools on the computer, open the dev server by IP and port on the same network, or use Xcode Simulator.

caveats: Self-promotion: the page opens with a plug for the author's aiforui.dev course, plugs Animations on the Web in the Motion section, and ends with a plug for animations.dev, where this component is built.
The article says the library is not finished and notes will be added as it matures; the publish date is unknown, so details may be dated.
The theme-bar sync is explicitly an unshipped idea: it is not in Vaul because it does not match the overlay when frames drop.
The visualViewport code is simplified by the author, declares unused variables (keyboardHeight, drawerHeight) and leaves OFFSET undefined; the approach has a slight delay.
The interpolateColor snippet references `linear` and `easing` without defining them, and the function name getNonTrasparentOverlayColor is misspelled in the source.
Preferring a drawer to a modal on mobile is the author's stated preference, not a measured finding.
The media list has one image (Xcode Simulator with the Vaul site); it was described from alt text and not downloaded. Videos and the interactive Family demo were not available in the raw text.
The prose says the keyboard handling relies on a "change" event, but the code listens for the visualViewport "resize" event.
Code in the raw text has extraction spacing (for example 'cubic-bezier ( 0.32 , 0.72 , 0 , 1 )'); code values here are written without those spaces and match the raw text once whitespace is ignored.

Not from this article: learn/sources.json records that the Vaul README says the library is unmaintained (checked 2026-09-24), so treat Vaul as a craft reference rather than a dependency to recommend [inferred].
